summary: This experimental document gives definitions, originally in RFC 1495 and RFC 1341, for carrying ODA (Office Document Architecture) in MIME and translating it to its X.400 representation.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2161 defines how an Office Document Architecture document can be represented as a MIME body part. It explains the labels used to describe the document and how those labels map to an X.400 ODA body part.

questions: how to send oda documents in email
how does mime carry oda documents
subtitle: The application/oda MIME type carries Office Document Architecture data.

tldr.problem: Mail systems need a way to carry Office Document Architecture data as a MIME body part and map it to the corresponding X.400 body part.
tldr.mechanism: The application/oda content type uses profile and class parameters to describe the ODA document; Base64 is suitable for carrying its data.
tldr.outcome: The RFC records the MIME representation and parameter mapping for ODA. It is Experimental.

today: RFC 2161 defines an Experimental MIME representation for ODA. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: ODA as a MIME Body Part
sections.content:
This RFC collects definitions previously contained in RFC 1495 and RFC 1341 for carrying Office Document Architecture (ODA) in MIME and translating it to its X.400 representation. The MIME subtype is application/oda, and its body contains information encoded using the ODA Interchange Format representation.

The Content-Type line identifies the document application profile with profile and the document class with class.
sections.plainLanguage: The application/oda MIME type marks a message part as an ODA document. Its header also labels the document profile and class.

sections.title: The Content-Type Parameters
sections.content:
The class parameter can be formatted, processable, or formatted-processable. The RFC gives Content-Type: application/oda; profile=Q112; class=formatted as an example. Base64 content-transfer-encoding is appropriate for carrying ODA.

If parameters are missing when a MIME part is mapped to X.400, the gateway uses profile Q112 and class formatted-processable. A gateway may try to obtain these values from the document, but the RFC does not require it.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIME header names the document profile and one of three document classes. If those labels are missing during conversion to X.400, the RFC specifies default values.

sections.title: Mapping Between MIME and X.400
sections.content:
For X.400-to-MIME mapping, the X.400 document application profile becomes the MIME profile parameter, and the architecture class becomes the MIME class parameter. The ODA data part becomes the body of the MIME content type.

For MIME-to-X.400 mapping, the parameters set the corresponding X.400 values. The RFC also says the document application profile and the ODA object identifier must be added to the message envelope's Encoded Information Types parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway copies the profile and class labels between the MIME header and the X.400 body-part parameters. It carries the ODA data as the MIME body.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that ODA can contain complex structures whose capabilities may be difficult to determine. ODA can also be extended with new content portions, so the threats associated with this body part could change over time.

The RFC says that no security risks related to ODA are known at the time it was written.
sections.plainLanguage: An ODA document may have complex or newly added content. The RFC reports no known ODA security risks at the time it was written.
